text:
Miles Thornton: Dropping first cut of the incident clustering sheet (last ~2 quarters). This is the thing we’ll use to justify the top-level taxonomy categories.

Link: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1rwi-redwood-sre-incidents-clustering (sheet: "2024Q4-2025Q1 clustering v0")

Pls help validate two things:
1) Top 10 categories feel right / missing anything obvious
2) Mislabels: if you see rows that are clearly wrong, comment w/ correct category + why

I took a pass on ~120 incidents; expect some jank esp. around "capacity" vs "routing" and "runtime crash" vs "model-specific instability".

Columns you’ll care about:
- `Candidate Category (v0)`
- `Impacted surface` (Hosted/Dedicated/Private)
- `Primary service` (routing, scheduler, gateway, fleet, etc.)
- `Contrib factors` (deploy, config, upstream provider, etc.)

If you only have time for 10 mins: please scan the "Top categories" pivot tab + spot-check 5 rows you recognize.

Deadline: comments by Wed EOD so we can lock v1 list for the incident-bot fields.

:eyes:

Sean Gallagher: ty Miles. Everyone: please don’t bikeshed granularity in-sheet — leave comments + we’ll resolve in the taxonomy review. We just need signal on what breaks most + where ownership is ambiguous.

Aisha Bello: Looking now. Quick question: are we counting “degraded mode / fallback” incidents separately or as contributing factor? I see a few labeled as “routing failure” but the customer impact was mostly “fallback to slower model”.

Miles Thornton: Good catch. For now I labeled by *primary customer impact mechanism*.
- If routing/policy couldn’t route => “Routing/policy failure”
- If routing intentionally fell back due to capacity => “Capacity exhaustion” w/ “fallback triggered” as contributing factor
But I’m not confident that’s consistent across rows. Mark them.

Allison Grant: Can we standardize the “region” values? I’m seeing us-east-1, use1, and "NA-East" in different rows (probably copied from postmortems).

Miles Thornton: Yeah, that’s a known mess. Mei and I will normalize the region column in backfill. For now comments are fine; we’ll map to canonical region codes when we ingest into dashboards.

Mei Lin: +1. I have a quick script to map the common aliases once we agree on the list (use1/us-east-1/etc.).

Irene Choi: Scanning pivot tab. Infra POV: “Capacity exhaustion” seems to include a bunch of cases that were actually “fleet provisioning / GPU host failures” (e.g., nodes flapping, bad AMI, k8s drain storms) vs demand overflow.

I’d prefer:
- “Fleet availability / host failures” (or similar)
- “Capacity exhaustion / autoscaling” only when demand > available and scaling didn’t keep up

Otherwise we’ll keep getting paged for routing spikes that are actually load-shedding/policy.

Miles Thornton: +1 that’s exactly the boundary question. Please drop examples row-by-row; we’ll carve the taxonomy definitions accordingly.

Mina Haddad: I’m looking at the ones tagged “Routing overload.” Some are actually “policy regression” (a deploy changed tier weights / region allowlist) not overload.

Example rows 44, 57, 61 in the sheet — those were config pushes that caused 5xx even though capacity was fine. I’d tag those “Routing/policy regression” with contrib factor “config/deploy.”

Rafael Mendes: This is super helpful — please note whether the right owner would’ve been different (routing oncall vs platform control plane vs infra). That’s part of why we’re doing this.

Sergio Costa: For reporting: can we keep the top-level category count <= 12? Dashboards get noisy fast. Maybe we keep “policy regression” under “Routing/control plane” as a subtype?

Miles Thornton: yep. The sheet has “Candidate Category (v0)” and “Subcategory (notes)” for that reason. Top-level should stay small.

Mateo Alvarez: Runtime scan. A bunch labeled “runtime crash” were actually model-specific (only llama3-70b-q4_k_m would OOM / assert) and would not repro on other models.

Would propose:
- “Runtime engine crash” = serving process dies / assertion / segfault (generally affects many models)
- “Model-specific instability” = a particular model build/quant profile causes crashes/ooms

Row 73 is definitely model-specific (bad quant profile). Row 79 is engine crash (cuda kernel assert) and should be runtime.

Sofia Ivanova: +1 to Mateo. Also some labeled “scheduler regression” are actually “queueing/latency due to batching config” — not a regression, just wrong knobs for the traffic profile.

Maybe “Scheduling/batching misconfiguration” as contrib factor rather than category? Depends on how we want to page.

Sean Gallagher: Reminder: taxonomy should help you page the right team *during the incident*. If it doesn’t change first responder, it probably shouldn’t be a top-level category.

So: runtime crash vs model-specific instability probably changes responder (runtime vs applied-ml/model onboarding). But “batching misconfig” might still be runtime/scheduling.

Dev Patel: From support side: anything that looks like “timeouts/5xx” is what we see first. If we can get a consistent split between:
- gateway/edge issues (streaming disconnects, 499s)
- routing/control plane errors
- capacity saturation
that helps us pick playbook + comms.

There are a few in the sheet labeled “runtime latency” that were actually streaming disconnects. Those should be “edge/gateway streaming” IMO.

Allison Grant reacted with :100:

Miles Thornton: Dev can you tag specific rows? We had a couple where the only symptom was "stream dropped" and we guessed runtime.

Dev Patel: Yep. Rows 18 and 22 were the ones from SUP-1977-ish timeframe. Customer saw disconnects mid-stream, tokens stopped, retries worked. Eng notes said “gateway bug around chunked encoding.” I’ll comment on those rows.

Irene Choi: Added comments on rows 31/32/35 — those were host failures (bad GPU firmware rollout) not autoscaling.

Mina Haddad: Added comments on 44/57/61 + a couple more. Also: some are tagged “upstream provider” (OpenAI outage etc.) — are we tracking those? They affect customer comms but not always a Redwood fix.

Aisha Bello: I think we should track as a top-level category “External dependency / upstream provider” but mark “Redwood-controlled: no”. That way we can separate MTTR for things we actually control.

Rafael Mendes: Agree. But careful: if we fail open vs fail closed, it becomes our incident too. Maybe category = “External dependency” and contributing factor = “fallback behavior” or “insufficient circuit breaking.”

Miles Thornton: I’ll incorporate that into taxonomy guidance. In sheet, please comment on any rows where upstream was the trigger but we made it worse.

Sergio Costa: Also, can folks avoid editing category cells directly? Add comments. We’ll use comments as ground truth during normalization so we can keep a changelog of what changed.

Mei Lin: +1. Direct edits make it hard to reconcile when we snapshot.

Sean Gallagher: +1. Comments only. We’ll do final pass in a working session.

Miles Thornton: Thanks all. Summary of what I’m hearing:
- Split fleet host failures vs capacity/autoscaling
- Split routing overload vs routing/policy regression (subtype)
- Split runtime engine crash vs model-specific instability
- Add external dependency category (with Redwood-controlled flag)
- Fix mislabels around edge/gateway streaming vs runtime latency

Keep the comments coming through tomorrow. I’ll post a cleaned-up v0.2 pivot + proposed top-level list in this thread once we incorporate the obvious fixes.
